Performance

Solar panel orientation and shading, explained

North is not the only roof that works — and shade is rarely as harmless as it looks. How orientation, tilt and shadows shape what a system produces.

Published 15 July 2026Updated 15 October 20267 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

Two houses with identical bills, identical equipment and the same installer can end up with meaningfully different generation — because the roofs point different ways and cast different shadows. Orientation and shading are the two factors that most often decide whether a system over-delivers or quietly underperforms for twenty years.

Orientation: what each direction actually means

  • North — the classic best case: the most total generation across a year, centred on midday.
  • East — strong morning generation that decays through the afternoon. Suits households with morning-heavy use, and avoids afternoon summer heat peak dependence.
  • West — the mirror image: slower start, strong afternoon generation into the evening ramp. In many Australian climates the west plane pairs well with afternoon air-conditioning and late household load.
  • East–west split — arrays arranged across both planes flatten the generation curve and extend productive hours, often producing only slightly less than a single ideal north plane over the year.
  • South — the lowest yield of the four. Usually a last resort, unless the roof offers so much area that covering a south plane still adds usable generation, or the household is large enough to use every kilowatt hour.

The key insight for buyers: orientation shifts when generation happens more than it destroys how much happens. A west-facing system that generates slightly less per year but overlaps with expensive evening hours can outperform a north system in bill terms. The right question is not 'which roof is best?' but 'which roof best matches when we use power?'

Tilt: less dramatic than people expect

Output is fairly forgiving across a wide band of roof pitches — broadly speaking, anywhere between about 15° and 35°, the annual difference is modest. Steeper tilt favours winter sun angles; flatter tilt favours summer. Flat roofs need tilt frames to shed water, lift the modules and improve the angle — a small extra cost that earns its keep on the right roof.

For most residential projects, orientation and shade are worth agonising over; tilt is worth mentioning once and moving on with a standard mounting solution.

Shading: the quiet performance killer

A shadow that covers one panel does not simply remove that panel's contribution. On a string inverter, panels are wired in series, and the weakest panel can limit the current through the whole string. The practical result: a shadow over a small fraction of the array can cost several times its physical share of output, depending on the layout and electronics.

  • Trees are the most common culprits — and their shadows move through the day and the year. A deciduous tree is nearly harmless in winter for a north array but will shade a western plane in summer afternoons.
  • Chimneys, satellite dishes, vents and roof hardware cast small but disproportionately costly shadows on the panels adjacent to them.
  • Neighbouring buildings and future construction are worth considering, especially for ground-floor roofs or where development is likely.
  • Time matters: shade during the middle of the day, when irradiance peaks, costs more than the same shadow in the early morning or late afternoon.

How a shade assessment should be done

  1. Identify every object that can cast shade on each roof plane, and at what times of day.
  2. Consider the sun's path across seasons — not just the summer position at noon, and not just one site visit's snapshot, but how winter angles and summer afternoons differ.
  3. Measure or map the roof planes: area, pitch, direction, and the practical footprint after setbacks and access paths.
  4. Design the strings around the answers — splitting shaded and unshaded panels, choosing per-panel electronics where justified, or moving the array to a better plane.

Design responses to unavoidable shade

  • Split the array across multiple inputs (MPPTs) so shaded and unshaded groups do not drag each other down.
  • DC optimisers or microinverters isolate each panel's output — often the cleanest solution where shade is partial and unavoidable, at a higher component cost.
  • Relocate part of the array to a better plane, accepting a smaller total size for a higher yield per panel.
  • Prune or reposition the obstacle — with council or heritage rules in mind, and with the owner's consent when the tree is not yours.
  • Accept a lower modelled yield and size accordingly; a shade-affected design done honestly still beats an optimistic design sold with an inflated generation estimate.

The cheapest optimiser is a pruning saw

Where a manageable tree causes significant, predictable shade, trimming or removing it can be more cost-effective than any electronics — subject to council rules and, if the tree is not yours, the neighbour's consent. Get the shade re-assessed after any major pruning; the design may be able to change with it.

Key takeaways

  • Orientation shifts when generation occurs; east, west and split arrays are all viable.
  • Roof tilt matters far less than orientation and shade across a broad 15–35° band.
  • Shade on one panel can cost several panels' worth of output on a string system.
  • Good designs split strings or use per-panel electronics around shade rather than pretending it is not there.
  • Assess shade across seasons and times of day, not from a single snapshot.
